title: What is known about 1RB1LF_0RC0RB_0LD1RB_1LE0LB_0LA1LC_0LB---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LF_0RC0RB_0LD1RB_1LE0LB_0LA1LC_0LB---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state machine halts from blank tape. This page records what is established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.

The tape is two binary counters written in short words. A counter at the left end, with digits 1010 (0) and 1000 (1), counts through all its values once per round; between two of its increments the head goes right and decrements a second counter whose digits are the words 1100 (1) and 1010 1010 (0); each borrow of the second counter moves one word 110 from one run of them to another. When the first run is used up the configuration changes in a way that is not yet understood.
verdict: Decided by an outside Rocq proof: it never halts. Busycoq pull request 103 (Alex Havrilla of DeepMind, 2026-11-19) proves this in Rocq, and we compiled it here with Coq 8.20.1 on busycoq's BB6 branch: it uses no axioms (Print Assumptions), and its transition table is this machine. It is their proof, on busycoq's definitions of a machine and of halting, and busycoq's maintainer has not yet reviewed it. Everything else on this page is what this repository found on its own, which by itself leaves the question open.

The question is open. No halt in the first 1010 steps (C simulator). The regular rounds follow an exact law, checked on all 39 of them; the phase changes between runs of regular rounds (24 seen) have no rule yet, and a halt (F reading a 1) could only come from one of them.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: The left counter: increment and overflow, for every length
claims.text: Digits of four cells, 1 0 1 0 = 0 and 1 0 0 0 = 1, least significant on the right, followed by 1 0, with the head in E on the 0 after it. incr: L 1010 (1000)^n 1 E>0 R reaches L 1000 (1010)^n 1 0 C> R in 10n + 7 steps, for every n, L and R. overflow: from 0^inf (1000)^n 1 E>0 R the counter becomes n + 1 zero digits, 0^inf (1010)^(n+1) 1 0 C> R, in 10n + 13 steps (the head visits a new cell on the left in state F on the way).

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>10</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/tmrun.c runs 1010 steps from blank tape without a halt; at the end the tape holds 255 ones.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 394 cells have been visited and 225 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Where a halt can be
claims.text: A closed tape language of windows of 5 cells (tools/py/bbtools/ctl.py, closure checked by the script, not by Lean) contains every configuration reachable from blank tape, and its only halting configurations have F reading a 1 with F>1 1 1 0 1 0.

claims.title: The round law, on all 39 regular rounds up to 10<sup>10</sup> steps
claims.text: At the visits of the head, in state F, to the leftmost cell, the tape right of it reads, in words a = 1100, b = 110, c = 10, c^s H X_1 bb X_2 bb ... bb X_w b^m cc0 b^j, with a header H (ab, ababcc or abccbcc) and right-counter digits X = a (1) or cc (0), X_1 least significant, value v. With D = 2s/2 and t the number of borrows of D decrements from v (t = (D − v − 1) div 2w + 1), a round with m ≥ t (m > t when H is not ab) goes to (s + 2, H, v − D mod 2w, m − t, j + t). All 39 such rounds from step 1,756 to 1010 follow it exactly; within a phase t doubles, which is the doubling map (m, j) → (m − j − k, 2j + k) seen before.
claims.where: tmrun MACHINE 10000000000 at F L 5000 > fl.txt; python3 py/round_law.py fl.txt, output in py/round_law_1e10.txt

claims.title: Alternating ticks
claims.text: In the round from step 4,982 to 7,434 (s = 10) the head turns at the low end of the left counter 64 times; 32 of them are increments (turn counts 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 at the digit positions, as for a 5-digit binary counter run through all its values) and 32 go right and decrement the right counter (3 digits, 4 borrows, m from 5 to 1, j from 1 to 5).
claims.where: turn histogram of that round (bbtools.explore turns)

claims.title: The phase changes, and the question
claims.text: When m is too small for the next round (m < t) the round ends differently: from H = ab the left counter loses two digits (s − 4) and the header becomes ababcc or abccbcc (four times it stays ab with m + j growing by 4); from those headers the next visit has s + 2, header ab, one more right digit and m + j + 1. The new digits are not yet predicted. Whether the machine halts is open.

check: gcc -O2 -o tmrun tools/c/tmrun.c && ./tmrun 1RB1LF_0RC0RB_0LD1RB_1LE0LB_0LA1LC_0LB--- 10000000000 at F L 5000 > fl.txt

explainer.lede: This machine runs two binary counters at once. One at the left end counts through all its values in each round; between two of its steps the head runs right and takes one from a second counter, and each borrow of that counter moves one word from one pile to another. Nobody knows whether it halts: it has run 10<sup>10</sup> steps without halting.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator.
Increment and overflow of the left counter, proved in Lean for every length.
Regular rounds that follow the round law exactly.

sections.heading: Two counters and two piles
html: Stop the machine each time the head stands on the leftmost cell in state F, and read the tape right of it in the words a = 1100, b = 110, c = 10. It reads
c^s  H  X_1 bb X_2 bb … bb X_w  b^m  cc0  b^j

• c^s is a binary counter set to 0: its digits are four cells, 1010 for 0 and 1000 for 1, the lowest on the right. Lean proves how it counts: the carry runs left over the 1-digits, turning them into 0-digits, and sets the first 0-digit (incr); when every digit is 1 it runs off the end and the counter starts again at 0 with one digit more (overflow).
• H is a short header, almost always ab.
• X_1 … X_w is a second binary counter, with digit a for 1 and cc for 0, the lowest on the left.
• b^m and b^j are two piles of the word b, separated by the marker cc0.

In one round the left counter runs through all its 2s/2 values. Between two of its increments the head runs right once and subtracts one from the second counter. Each time that counter passes from 0 to its largest value (a borrow), one b moves from the first pile to the second. At the end of the round the left counter overflows: the head reaches a new cell on the left in state F, and the counter is two cells longer (s + 2).

So a round sends t words from pile m to pile j, where t is the number of borrows in 2s/2 subtractions. In the next round there are twice as many subtractions, so t doubles: this is the doubling seen at the left end, (m, j) → (m − t, j + t) with t twice as large each round. All 39 such rounds up to 1010 steps follow it exactly (py/round_law.py).

stepper.tape: F> 0 c^{s} ab X b^{m} cc0 b^{j}   (X fixed; t borrows this round)

rules.name: Regular round
rules.text: The round law, checked on all 39 regular rounds to 1010 steps (py/round_law.py); the counter steps inside it are proved in Lean (incr, overflow).

stepper.note: Starts at the visit at step 54,454,224 (s = 30, m = 33, j = 1, and t = 4 borrows in the coming round). Three regular rounds follow, to (s, m, j) = (36, 5, 29) at step 72,347,964, as in the machine; then t = 32 > m and the next round is a phase change, which the stepper does not model. The stepper does arithmetic only.

sections.heading: Phase changes
html: When the first pile is too small for the next round (m < t) the round ends differently. From the header ab the left counter comes back two digits shorter (s − 4) and the header becomes ababcc or abccbcc; from those headers the next visit has s + 2, the header ab again, one more digit in the second counter, and one more b in the piles. 24 phase changes happened up to 1010 steps; the new digits of the second counter are not yet predicted, so the run cannot yet be followed past them by arithmetic.
A halt needs F to read a 1, and a closed tape language of 5-cell windows confines it to F>1 1 1 0 1 0; the regular rounds never produce it, so the question is decided in the phase changes.

sections.heading: Where a halt could happen
html: The machine stops when F reads a 1. A closed tape language with windows of 5 cells, which contains every configuration reachable from blank tape, adds that the five cells right of the head must read 1 1 0 1 0: F>1 1 1 0 1 0.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.093). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.087).
After 109 steps the tape spans 394 cells (289 left of the start, 84 right), with a density of 1s of 0.571.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

family: Two binary counters fed by alternating ticks, with borrows moving words between two runs (exp/exp; phase changes not modelled)
summary: Two binary counters fed by alternating ticks: a left counter that counts through all its values once per round and a right counter whose borrows move one 110 word from one run to another; the round law (s, X, m, j) -> (s+2, X - 2^(s/2), m - t, j + t) holds on all 39 regular rounds to 10^10 steps, the counter rules are proved in Lean, the phase changes are not understood; open. Decided outside: busycoq PR 103 proves in Rocq that it never halts (compiled here).
